title: The odd prayer
hook: the odd-numbered night prayer, strongly stressed, wajib in the Hanafi school

segments.voice: Yesterday, rawatib, and your line: the sunnah around it. Did you add one small extra thing before or after something you had to do? Today, the extra prayer that closes the day. Day one thousand eighty-one.

Abu Hurayrah once said his close friend had advised him to keep three things until he died. His close friend was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The three: fasting three days every month, praying two units in the late morning, and praying witr before going to sleep. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the list, at number 1178. Two of those are about daylight. The last is about the moment just before you turn out the light, when the phone is on the charger and the day is nearly done. Of everything he could have been told to hold on to, one item was a short prayer at the edge of sleep.
screen: `ADVICE TO KEEP UNTIL DEATH.` → `FAST, PRAY IN THE MORNING, PRAY WITR.` → `A PRAYER AT THE EDGE OF SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Witr means odd, as in an odd number. It's the prayer with an odd count of units that closes the night's praying. One unit, or three, or more, so long as the total comes out odd. Why odd? In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 6410, the Prophet ﷺ says that Allah is witr, and loves witr. The same word that names this prayer is used of God: single, one, not paired. Some teachers read ending the night on an odd number as a small sign of that oneness, the tawhid this path has already met, written into the shape of a prayer. When is it prayed? Any time after the night prayer, isha, until dawn. In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 998, he says: make witr the last of your prayer at night. And Sahih Muslim, number 755, gives a practical choice. Whoever fears they won't wake in the last part of the night should pray witr at the start of it, before sleeping. Whoever expects to wake can pray it at the end, because prayer at the end of the night is witnessed. That's Abu Hurayrah's choice in the hook: witr before sleep, so it's never lost. How binding is it? Here the schools differ, and they say so openly. The Hanafi school holds witr to be wajib, necessary, a step below the obligatory prayers but not to be dropped. The other Sunni schools hold it to be a strongly stressed sunnah, not obligatory. Either way, it's the prayer the day ends on.
screen: `WITR: AN ODD NUMBER OF UNITS.` · `ALLAH IS WITR AND LOVES WITR.` · `LAST OF THE NIGHT, OR BEFORE SLEEP.` · `WAJIB FOR HANAFIS, STRONGLY STRESSED FOR OTHERS.` · then, large: `MAKE WITR THE LAST OF YOUR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray one witr, or sit as if the day were closing. Settle, and let the day slow down. If you pray, you can decide now to pray witr tonight before sleep, even a single unit, so the night ends on it. If you don't, try this instead: count your breaths, slowly, one, two, three, and stop on an odd number. One last breath, alone, unpaired. Then rest in what's left of the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Witr. Odd. The prayer with an odd number of units that ends the night, wajib for the Hanafi school and strongly stressed for the other Sunni schools. Today's word.
Your line: end the night odd. Today, when you finish something, mark the finish with one breath, single and deliberate, before you move on. Tomorrow, the night prayer. Day one thousand eighty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims pray witr after the night prayer and before dawn, as one, three or more units so the total is odd; some pray it before sleep and some at the end of the night, and the Hanafi school counts it as wajib while the other Sunni schools treat it as a strongly stressed sunnah.

original.note: Arabic: odd, single; the odd-numbered night prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: witr is just one more prayer at night.
what it means: an odd-numbered prayer that ends the night, before sleep or before dawn.
what a scholar hears: Allah is witr and loves witr (Bukhari 6410), with the Hanafi school holding it wajib and the other Sunni schools a strongly stressed sunnah.

notes: Hadith numbers and details to confirm: Bukhari 1178 (Abu Hurayrah's three pieces of advice: three days' fasting each month, two rak'ahs of duha, witr before sleeping); Bukhari 6410 (Allah is witr and loves witr; also Muslim 2677); Bukhari 998 (Ibn 'Umar: make witr the last of your night prayer); Muslim 755 (Jabir: witr at the start of the night if you fear not waking; prayer at the end of the night is witnessed).
'The same word that names this prayer is used of God' is a reading of Bukhari 6410, not an etymology claim; confirm the phrasing ('single, one, not paired').
Ja'fari practice (witr as a single unit at the end of the night prayer, often with qunut) is not described; Keeper may add.
Witr's time is given as after isha until dawn; Hanafi and others differ on details (e.g. praying it with isha combined). Confirm.
